claim: Women and minoritized groups are more likely than other demographic groups to leave careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.
source: The 'leaky pipeline' is a metaphor that describes a persistent problem in which certain demographic groups, particularly women and minoritized groups, are more likely than other demographic groups to leave careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Hinton et al., 2020; Hinton and Lambert, 2022; Jackson, 2023; Lin, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The leaky pipeline reduces diversity in STEM fields.
source: In addition to depleting the pool of available talent in these subjects, the leaky pipeline also reduces diversity (Sarraju et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sarraju et al., 2023.

claim: The leaky pipeline hinders scientific progress.
source: the leaky pipeline also reduces diversity (Sarraju et al., 2023) and hinders scientific progress (Hofstra et al., 2020).

claim: Almost one-third of students who leave a PhD program do so during their first year.

claim: There is an opportunity to reduce leaks in the pipeline during the first year of graduate school.

source: We encourage graduate schools and programs in the life sciences and medicine at other universities to organize their own symposia on the 'hidden curriculum' to help address the unique challenges that URG students face in graduate school (Hinton et al., 2020; Sarraju et al., 2023; Allen-Ramdial and Campbell, 2014; Mays et al., 2023), and to reduce the number of students who quit PhDs during their first year (Golde, 1998; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' experience and supported by citations about challenges faced by URG students.

claim: Organizing hidden curriculum symposia could help reduce the number of students who quit PhDs during their first year.
source: We encourage graduate schools and programs in the life sciences and medicine at other universities to organize their own symposia on the 'hidden curriculum' to help address the unique challenges that URG students face in graduate school (Hinton et al., 2020; Sarraju et al., 2023; Allen-Ramdial and Campbell, 2014; Mays et al., 2023), and to reduce the number of students who quit PhDs during their first year (Golde, 1998; Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the symposium's positive effects and the known problem of first-year attrition.
